1.explanation: The core of ESLint’s indent rule lives in lib/rules/indent.js. That file contains the logic for computing expected indentation levels for nested expressions, including logical operators and parenthesized sub-expressions. In version 4.1.0 this logic was changed and no longer accounts properly for the combination of parentheses and JSX tokens within a binary expression, which causes the offset error. The legacy implementation in lib/rules/indent-legacy.js follows a similar computation and also needs adjustment for consistency or as a reference fallback. Both files must be updated so that parenthesized JSX expressions in logical contexts get the same base indentation as unwrapped JSX expressions.
1.bug_scenario: When you use a parenthesized JSX element on the right side of a logical binary expression inside JSX (for example b && (<div>…)), ESLint’s new 4.1.0 indent rule miscalculates the expected column. It applies an extra indent level to the opening <div> inside the parentheses so you see errors like “Expected indentation of 16 spaces but found 20.” If you remove the parentheses or don’t use JSX there, the indentation is correct.

2.explanation: Both lib/rules/indent.js and its companion lib/rules/indent-legacy.js implement the core logic of ESLint’s indent rule, including handling of multi-line expressions, nested blocks, and JSX. The regression manifests only when a binary expression is parenthesized around JSX. Those two files contain the code paths that calculate expected indentation offsets for parenthesized expressions and JSX elements, so they must be updated to correctly account for the extra layer of parentheses around the JSX in that scenario.
2.bug_scenario: When using ESLint’s built-in indent rule (version 4.1.1) on JSX code that contains a binary expression wrapped in parentheses (e.g. b && ( <div> … )), the rule erroneously computes the wrong indent level for the lines inside the parentheses. In ESLint 4.0 intact, the code indented correctly, but in 4.1.0 it reports “Expected indentation of 16 spaces but found 20,” etc. Removing the parentheses or unwrapping the JSX out of the binary expression causes the rule to pass again.
